findings.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The merry heart is a threshold state. In every narrative it comes after eating and drinking and immediately before a decisive event, which others usually initiate. The good heart lowers guard. What enters at that moment decides the outcome: murder (Amnon); exposure and anger (Vashti, Ahasuerus); mockery turned to catastrophe (Samson); outrage (Gibeah); approach and redemption (Ruth); a dead heart the next morning (Nabal); God's claim on the soul (the rich fool); The heart's condition swings overnight. Nabal: merry heart → dead heart (1Sa 25:36–37). Ahasuerus: merry heart → burning anger (Est 1:10–12). The heart's state is not stable; wine sets it high, and news or refusal drops it.; 1Ki 21 joins spirit and heart. Ahab's spirit is vexed and he stops eating. Jezebel prescribes food and a good heart, secured by injustice. A spirit-state is "cured" by manufacturing a heart-state — the only place in the batch where one is treated through the other.; Positive merriment exists outside the narratives: "they … went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown" (1Ki 8:66); "A joyful heart is good medicine" (Pro 17:22); "A glad heart makes a cheerful face" (Pro 15:13); "let your heart cheer you … But know that … God will bring you into judgment" (Ecc 11:9); When the heart is good because of God, no threshold event follows. When it is good from wine, one does.; Revisit (Batch G) — the threshold pattern extended: The step before the merry heart: "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5, 8). The father-in-law alternates *strengthen* (5, 8) and *merry* (6, 9). Each round delays departure (G §3.1).; The threshold engineered and refused: David "made him drunk" (2Sa 11:13). Uriah, who had sworn "as your soul lives, I will not do this thing" (11:11), still does not go home. The next morning: the death letter (11:14–15) (G §4).; The soul's version: "prepare for me delicious food … that my soul may bless you" (Gen 27:4). "He ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank" (27:25) → the irreversible blessing of the false firstborn → Esau's hatred "in his heart" (27:41; §8.2 below) (G §13.3).; The Samson sequence in full (Judg 16:15–30): soul vexed (16); heart told (17); strength and the Lord gone (19–20); the Philistines' merry hearts (25); strength asked for (28)

findings.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: "let my soul die" (30); The merry-heart threshold is the penultimate step (G §3.6).; The counter-case: the sad heart at a feast.; Hannah "would not eat … why is your heart sad?" → prays "after they had eaten and drunk" → is taken for drunk → "troubled in spirit … pouring out my soul" → face no longer sad (1Sa 1:7–18).; Nehemiah: "when wine was before him … Why is your face sad? … sadness of the heart" → prayer → request granted (Neh 2:1–5).; The sad heart at the feast is also a threshold, but what enters is prayer, and the outcome is a gift (G §8.2).; Revisit (Batch H §7.6) — the threshold pattern extended again: Esther's wine-banquets (Est 5:6–14; 7:3–8): "as they were drinking wine after the feast" (5:6) → Haman goes out "joyful and glad of heart" (5:9) → sees Mordecai → wrath → "all this is worth nothing to me" (5:13) → the gallows (5:14).; At the second banquet Esther asks for her life (7:3). The king "arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking" (7:7), and Haman begs for his life (7:7–8).; One banquet is the threshold for two outcomes: Esther's petition is granted; Haman falls.; The threshold refused at the heart: "Daniel resolved [*set on his heart*] that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank" (Dan 1:8) → "fatter in flesh" than those who ate it (1:15). Compare Uriah (point 5).; The inner sentence comes first: "if that servant says to himself, 'My master is delayed,' and begins … to eat and drink and get drunk" → the master comes "on a day when he does not expect him" (Luk 12:45–46; Mat 24:48–51).; The warning: "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34).; The counter-statement: "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17).; Revisit (Batch G v3 §16) — the threshold and death: Nabal's sequel: the heart dies in the morning (1Sa 25:37), and "about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (25:38). The dead heart comes before the dead man.

But they did not continue doing it" (Num 11:25); "the Spirit rested on them … and so they prophesied in the camp" (Num 11:26); "The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding" (Isa 11:2); "the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you" (1Pe 4:14); "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (2Ki 2:15)

Context Num 11:24–29 — the resting Spirit resisted and defended: The Spirit taken from Moses rests on the seventy; they prophesy "but they did not continue" (25).; Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp (26). Joshua: "My lord Moses, stop them" (28).; Moses: "Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the Lord's people were prophets, that the Lord would put his Spirit on them!" (29).

findings.text: Context 2Ki 2:9–15 — the resting spirit confirmed by others: "Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me" (9); "You have asked a hard thing; yet, if you see me as I am being taken … it shall be so" (10); Elijah goes up; Elisha sees, cries out and tears his clothes (11–12); Takes up the cloak, strikes the water: "Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?" The water parts (13–14); The sons of the prophets: "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (15); [Claude reading] The request (9) is granted on condition of seeing (10). Elisha's first act is a question to God, not a claim of power (14). The resting of the spirit is recognised by others from its effect (15), not asserted by its bearer. Num 11 has the same shape: others see and report (27).

findings.text: Revisit: Batch E §2 recorded 2Ki 2:9 only as "asking for another's spirit". Its outcome in 2:15 is part of the same relation.

Holding the spirit back — the wise and the fool: "A fool gives full vent to his spirit [*temper*], but a wise man quietly holds it back" (Pro 29:11) [T]. "calmness will lay great offenses to rest" (Ecc 10:4) [T].

Silence that ratifies: "her father hears of her vow and of her pledge by which she has bound herself [*her nephesh*] and says nothing to her, then all her vows shall stand" (Num 30:4, 7, 11). With Batch E §9.1 (the vow annulled, and "the Lord will forgive her"): a soul-binding vow hangs on another person's speech or silence on the day he hears it.

Peace guarding hearts: Context Phili 4:6–7: "do not be anxious … let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God … will guard your hearts and your minds"; "let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts" (Col 3:15); "Peace I leave with you … Let not your hearts be troubled" (Joh 14:27); "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (Joh 16:33)

False peace declared in the heart: "blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe [*have peace*], though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'" (Deu 29:19); "to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come'" (Jer 23:17); "saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life" (Jer 4:10); "who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts" (Psa 28:3)
Peace of the whole person: "the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless" (1Th 5:23) [H1].
Flesh and peace: "no flesh has peace" (Jer 12:12); "to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace" (Rom 8:6).

10. Gentleness — the spirit as the manner of approach: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?" (1Co 4:21) [X]; "you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself" (Gal 6:1) [X]; "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4) [H1]; "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29); "receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:21); "make a defense … with gentleness and respect, having a good conscience" (1Pe 3:15–16); [Claude reading] "Spirit" here names the manner in which one person comes to another (1Co 4:21; Gal 6:1) — the disposition [X] governing an encounter. Where gentleness is located in the heart (Mat 11:29), it is a settled character. Where it is "of spirit", it is the bearing brought to a specific meeting.

findings.text: 11. The good heart and the good conscience: "an honest and good heart" that holds the word fast (Luk 8:15); "the good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good" (Luk 6:45; Mat 12:34)
Good conscience: 1Ti 1:5, 19; 1Pe 3:16, 21 ("an appeal to God for a good conscience"); Act 23:1; Heb 13:18

11. The good heart and the good conscience: "I have the desire to do what is right … nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh" (Rom 7:18); "it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods" (Heb 13:9); "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God' … there is none who does good" (Psa 14:1; 53:1)
Good toward one's own soul: "His soul shall abide in well-being [*good*]" (Psa 25:13); "delight yourselves [*your nephesh*] in rich food" (Isa 55:2).

12.1 The heart's own purpose inside God's purpose: "But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few" (Isa 10:7); [Claude reading] Assyria is the Lord's rod (Isa 10:5), but its heart has its own intention. The instrument's heart does not share the purpose of the one who wields it. This underlies the judgment on the instrument that follows (10:12 — Batch D §9.1, "the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria").

findings.text: 12.2 The heart devising and muttering violence — one verb, opposite content: *hāgâ* "mutter, meditate" [lexical]: "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things" (Pro 15:28); "for their hearts devise [*mutter*] violence, and their lips talk of trouble" (Pro 24:2); "conceiving and uttering from the heart lying words" (Isa 59:13); "Your heart will muse on the terror" (Isa 33:18); "those who seek my life … meditate treachery all day long" (Psa 38:12); [Claude reading] The heart's inner murmuring is the same act for the righteous and the violent. Its content (how to answer / violence / lies / terror) decides its moral character. The heart is an organ of rehearsal.; Also: "who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually" (Psa 140:2); "in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence" (Psa 58:2); "war was in his heart" (Psa 55:21).

12.3 Soul, body and the one who destroys: "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell" (Mat 10:28); "The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you" (Rev 18:14); "God said … 'I have determined to make an end of all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence'" (Gen 6:13); "the breath of the ruthless is like a storm against a wall" (Isa 25:4) [*breath*]; "they breathe out violence" (Psa 27:12)

Devoted to destruction (*ḥērem*, §0.2): "every person [*nephesh*] in it … he left none remaining" (Jos 10:28–39); "there was none left that breathed" (Jos 11:11); "it was the Lord's doing to harden their hearts … in order that they should be devoted to destruction" (Jos 11:20). Hardened hearts precede the ban.

findings.text: 12.3 Soul, body and the one who destroys: "he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children … lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction [*ḥērem*]" (Mal 4:6). The turning of hearts is the alternative to the ban.

13. Encouragement and building up (M52): "the church … walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied" (Act 9:31) [D1]; "waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him" (Luk 2:25) [D1]; "strive to excel in building up the church" (1Co 14:12); "building yourselves up … praying in the Holy Spirit" (Jude 20); "being built up as a spiritual house" (1Pe 2:5)

Building up a weak conscience into sin: "if anyone sees you … eating in an idol's temple, will he not be encouraged [*built up*], if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?" (1Co 8:10). [Claude reading] The vocabulary of edification is used ironically: example can "build up" a weak conscience in the wrong direction.

14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch F [Claude reading]: Relating to others is most often a matter of the soul.; Souls are knit (1Sa 18:1).; A soul loves, seeks and fails (Song 3; 5).; Malice lives in the soul (Eze 25:6, 15).; Souls abhor each other, even God's soul and the people's (Lev 26).; One loves another "as one's own soul".; The heart is where hatred starts and is spoken (Lev 19:17; Gen 27:41). It is also where the response to another's fall is judged (Pro 24:17).; The human spirit registers bonds and bearing.; It is unsettled by a friend's absence and refreshed by a friend's arrival (2Co 2:13; 7:13; 1Co 16:18).; It is the manner of approach — gentleness (1Co 4:21).; It is what the wise hold back and the fool vents (Pro 29:11).; Sequences matter more than single verses. Reading before and after changed the picture in six places: 1Sa 18 (Jonathan and Saul); Lev 26 (reciprocal abhorrence broken by God); Psa 143 and Psa 51 (the crushing chains); Judg 19 and the other merry-heart narratives (threshold states); 2Co 2 → 7 (the spirit's rest through persons); 2Ki 2 (spirit transfer confirmed by others); Meaning shifts with circumstance in consistent ways: *crush*: by whom, and turned to whom (§5); *tender heart*: to what it yields (§6); *good heart*: from God or from wine (§7); *love / hate one's soul*: well-being vs clinging (§3); *hāgâ*: what the heart rehearses (§12.2); *nûaḥ*: what rests in or on the person (§9.5); Inner states spread between people: the fainthearted soldier melts others (Deu 20:8); heart-speech is reported (Gen 27:42); a lowly heart gives rest to other souls (Mat 11:29); a congregation refreshes Titus's spirit (2Co 7:13); the prophet's heart takes in the people's doom (Jer 4:18–19); Other spirits relate to people as occupants of a house (Mat 12:43–45) and as seizures between people (1Sa 18:10; Judg 9:23 in Batch D). The divine Spirit rests upon people and is recognised by others (Num 11; 2Ki 2).; Fringe worth keeping: the knit soul beside the seizing spirit in one chapter (1Sa 18); the heart awake while the body lags (Song 5); God refusing to complete reciprocal abhorrence (Lev 26:44); Jezebel curing a vexed spirit by a manufactured good heart (1Ki 21); the prophet's heart for Moab set against Ammon's malice of soul (Isa 15; Jer 48; Eze 25); past hatred as a legal criterion (Deu 19)
